characters: Seyram: a 13-year-old girl in a school uniform, with braids, holding a library book.
Yaro: her classmate, 13, in a white shirt, drawing maps.
Mr Ayitey: their history teacher, in a brown jacket, with a globe.
Plato: an ancient Greek thinker in a white robe, writing on a scroll (story picture).
Atlantis: a shining island city with round harbours, golden walls and a big temple, sinking into dark waves.

narrationPlan.voice: Dreamy storyteller voice for the legend; Mr Ayitey is calm and exact for the facts
narrationPlan.pace: Dreamy and curious, with a firm tone for the evidence (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Gentle waves and a dreamy harp, darkening at the sinking, then clear and thoughtful (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Atlantis is a Greek story, not a Ghanaian one. The pupils and teacher are invented. Ghanaian pupils can compare it with stories in their own communities about places that vanished, such as drowned towns or lost cities.
The story uses Atlantis to show how historians separate what a source says from what evidence supports.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check the description of Plato’s text against a named source: Timaeus and Critias (4th century BCE); beyond the Pillars of Hercules; “larger than Libya and Asia together”; sank in “a day and a night”.
Check the Thera/Santorini dating (the source says about 1650–1550 BCE, so “about 3,500 years ago” is a rounded figure).
The wording “more than 2,300 years ago” is rounded from Plato’s dates (c. 429–347 BCE).

teacherGuide.overview: A mystery about a story: what the source says, what evidence exists, and why scholars disagree. It teaches the habit of separating “what is written” from “what is proven”.
learningGoals: Explain that Atlantis comes from a single writer, Plato.
Compare two explanations (invention and real event).
State what evidence would convince experts.

subjectLinks.subject: Geography
subjectLinks.link: The Mediterranean and the Strait of Gibraltar

beforeReading: Ask: do you know stories of places that vanished? Where did they come from?
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to underline “Plato wrote”.
afterReading: Mark the Strait of Gibraltar and Santorini on a map.
Write two columns: What the source says / What the evidence shows.
discussion: Why can a story be useful even if it did not happen?
What would make you believe a claim that Atlantis has been found?
reflection: Which part of history do you wish we had better evidence for?

mathsExtension.task: Plato lived around 429 to 347 BCE. About how many years did he live?
From 347 BCE to 2026 CE, about how many years is that? (There is no year 0.)

support: Provide a two-column chart: Plato said / Evidence shows.
stretch: Research one real sunken settlement and compare the evidence with Atlantis.

culturalNotes: Atlantis is a Greek story, not a Ghanaian one. The pupils and teacher are invented. Ghanaian pupils can compare it with stories in their own communities about places that vanished, such as drowned towns or lost cities.
The story uses Atlantis to show how historians separate what a source says from what evidence supports.
localiseThis: Invite elders to share local stories of drowned or vanished places and discuss what evidence could test them.
Treat every community’s stories with respect.

whatWeKnow: The earliest known account of Atlantis is by Plato in Timaeus and Critias.
There is no archaeological evidence for Atlantis as Plato described it.
The eruption at Thera (Santorini) was real but does not match Plato’s description.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Whether Plato invented the story or based it on older memories.

factCheck.claim: Plato described Atlantis in Timaeus and Critias: an island beyond the Pillars of Hercules, larger than Libya and Asia, defeated by Athens, then sunk by earthquakes and floods in an unbearable day and a night; no archaeological evidence exists; scholars see it as invention or a memory of a real event such as the Thera eruption (c. 1650–1550 BCE), which does not match in size or place.
